title: The ketubah read
hookLine: the marriage contract is read aloud under the chuppah
last: A HOUSE OPEN ON ALL SIDES.

cards: Under the canopy, the music has stopped. The couple stands close.

Someone steps forward with a large sheet of paper, sometimes plain, sometimes painted with flowers, birds, a border of Hebrew letters, and reads aloud, in Aramaic. Some guests follow every word; some only hear the rhythm.
At some weddings a translation comes after. It isn't a poem. It's a contract, with obligations and a sum of money in it.
Why stop a wedding, at the moment everyone is waiting for, to read out a legal document?

teach.b: Ketubah means, simply, the written thing. It's the marriage contract, and it sets out what the husband owes his wife. Where do those duties come from?

In Exodus, in a law about a man who takes a second wife, the Torah lists what he may not hold back from the first. In the King James wording: "her food, her raiment, and her duty of marriage, shall he not diminish."
Food, clothing, and closeness. The rabbis read that verse as a floor, not a ceiling: the least a marriage owes, written down so no one can pretend it was never said.
The ketubah also promises the wife a sum of money if the marriage ends, by divorce or by her husband's death. The Talmud gives the reason: so a husband couldn't send his wife away lightly.
In a world where a woman could be left with nothing, the rabbis put a cost on leaving and her name on the page. Why aloud?
The ketubah is signed by witnesses before the ceremony, then read in front of everyone, and a promise read out in a crowd is one the crowd can remember. Some hang their ketubah on a wall at home.
Some couples today choose one with promises from both sides, in words they've thought through together. Either way, love is the reason.
The writing is how it gets kept.

how: Before a Jewish wedding, witnesses sign the ketubah, the marriage contract; under the chuppah it is read aloud, traditionally in Aramaic, often followed by a translation, and some couples later display it at home.

games.q: you're one of the rabbis. a husband can end a marriage, and a wife could be left with nothing. what do you do?
o: write down a sum he owes her if the marriage ends.
leave it to her family to sort out.
games.why: the ketubah fixes a sum owed to her; the Talmud says it's so a husband can't send his wife away lightly.

practice: Bring to mind one promise you've made, written down or only meant, to a partner, a child, a friend, a parent, or yourself, and put it into one plain sentence.
If you're somewhere you can, say it quietly out loud, as if it were read under a canopy, and notice how it sounds outside your own head.

wordCard.voice: The ketubah read: the marriage contract, signed by witnesses and read aloud under the chuppah, so the promise is heard as well as written. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the written thing, the marriage contract; Ashkenazi Jews often say keh-SU-bah.

carryVoice: Your line: promised in writing. Love makes the promise; the ink helps it last. Tomorrow, the singing.
